blocks.heading: Digging beneath the surface; the Shem Havaya

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach compares the Torah to a field in South Africa: on the surface are beautiful flowers, but whoever digs finds gold, and deeper still, diamonds. So too pshat is gorgeous, yet those who dig find something more desirable, and he sets out to dig beneath the familiar customs of Tu B'Shvat.

Each month, he explains, has its own arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya. Yud-Kei are father and mother, Vav-Kei son and daughter, and the rule is that the masculine is chesed and the feminine din.

blocks.heading: Giver and receiver: chassan and kallah

paragraphs.text: The chassan is chesed, the giver, and the kallah din, the receiver. Therefore kiddushin works only when he gives to her, never the reverse, and only he writes a kesubah promising to give.

In the Name, the Yud and Vav are masculine letters and the two Heis feminine, which is why women's names such as Sarah and Rivkah end with a Hei. Since two of the four letters are identical, they can be arranged in exactly twelve ways, one for each month.

blocks.heading: In kedushah the masculine comes first

paragraphs.text: A further rule: in kedushah the masculine comes first. The Mashgiach brings Rashi that with Yaakov the passuk mentions his sons before his wives, while with Esav the wives come first, a sign of din. When the feminine leads it dominates and nullifies the chesed; when the masculine leads it sweetens the din.

Chesed is the right side and din the left, so in loshon hakodesh one writes from right to left, washes and dresses the right hand first, and ties the left shoe first to tie down the din. Esav writes from left to right, while the descendants of Avraham also write from right to left.

He adds that white is chesed, which the doctors wear without knowing why, and brings the Gemara that in kedushah men go first. He does not advocate changing accepted etiquette, but asks that those who keep this order not be criticized. Achashverosh, he says, got into trouble by letting the woman dominate, as with Vashti.

blocks.heading: Nissan and Tishrei, kings of the year

paragraphs.text: Some months show that chesed directs, the pleasant ones that are neither too hot nor too cold. The sefarim say to have the month's arrangement in mind, and the Mashgiach shows in a siddur passed around that each month has its arrangement and a passuk. Nissan is Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei, from the roshei teivos of 'Yismechu hashamayim v'sagel ha'aretz'.

Nissan, when flowers blossom and trees bud, rules the summer months; it goes in Aleph-Beis order, as hinted in 'chodesh ha'aviv'. Tishrei rules the harsher winter months and comes from the Aleph-Beis backwards, but through the avodah of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur its second half, from Sukkos, becomes Yud-Kei, chesed.

blocks.heading: Tammuz, Teves, and the turn on the fifteenth

paragraphs.text: Tammuz, the peak of summer, has the Name completely backwards, from the sofei teivos of 'zeh einenu shaveh li': din without seasoning. It is when the meraglim set out and the churban began, and its din lasts into Av until Chamishah Asar B'Av, when chesed returns.

Teves, the brunt of winter, is likewise reversed, and its din overlaps into Shevat. Shevat's first half is Hei-Yud, backwards, but its second half is Vav-Hei, already sweetened, from Tu B'Shvat. This is why the right side is always strengthened, as with the longer right strap of the tefillin.

Should one think only of the letters? The Mashgiach warns that this makes davening mechanical, as Rebbe Nachman of Breslov said of siddurim full of names. If it gives a lift, drawing down chesed and connecting one to Hashem, it is good; otherwise one should not do it. In Tammuz one sweetens the reversed Name by connecting to chesed.

blocks.heading: From Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos: the gates of chesed

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Chaim that from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos there are never two weeks without a Yom Tov: Rosh Chodesh Adar, Purim, Rosh Chodesh Nissan, Pesach, Pesach Sheini and on. It is an ascent of ever stronger chassadim, to be used for Torah and avodah, for now the gates of chesed are open, while in days of din one must crack them open.
Even when nothing shows on the tree, the sap is already rising through the roots.

blocks.heading: Havaya and Adnus: the union in the Mikdash

paragraphs.text: The Shem Havaya is chesed and the Shem Adnus din, chassan and kallah; together they are the union of Hakadosh Baruch Hu and Knesses Yisrael, seated in the Mikdash. In 'Mikdash Ad-nai konenu yadecha', read the day before, the Name is written Adnus. The siddurim join the two Names, the aim of all tefillos.
Tumah mimics kedushah like a monkey, with its own masculine and feminine, but there the feminine dominates.

blocks.heading: The two forces of tumah and the number 580

paragraphs.text: The Ohr HaChaim in Vayechi writes that tumah appeared to him in a dream as two dogs: the male he overpowered at once, the female only with difficulty and not completely.

The Mashgiach will not say their names aloud. Together they equal 580, the number of animals Yaakov sent Esav and the value of Seir. The two Names of kedushah, Havaya (26) and Adnus (65), equal 91, which is why one answers Amen.

blocks.heading: Seraf in the ilan; davening for the esrog

paragraphs.text: Rashi says that by Tu B'Shvat the seraf, sap, rises in the ilan, tree. Seraf is 580 and ilan 91: the power of tumah weakens and is raised into kedushah, and the fruits that begin to grow will become holy through a berachah. Nissan, Purim and Pesach are approaching.

On Tu B'Shvat one davens for an esrog, as chesed begins to operate. The Bnei Yissaschar and the minhag recorded in Shulchan Aruch speak of making borei pri ha'etz, and the Mashgiach adds a remez: one has in mind the pri etz hadar, since through the four minim, as the Midrashim say, comes Klal Yisrael's success.

blocks.heading: Barren trees, and only scratching the surface

paragraphs.text: Repeating from the day before, the Mashgiach brings Rashi on 'the tree of the field will give its fruit': even barren trees will bear fruit, for all trees were made fruitful until Adam's sin. Tu B'Shvat is a time to daven for them.
He closes that all such insights only scratch the surface; until Mashiach comes, what was said is a drop in the ocean.
